issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette:
# Thom's Hypervigilance

Thom Seng was forty-eight years old when the tank rupture changed everything. He had been an HVAC technician for twenty-six years by then, methodical and detail-oriented, the kind of worker whose clients requested him by name. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, he was called to a commercial warehouse in the industrial district to service the cooling system for a chemical storage facility. The job was routine—he had done it a dozen times. But this time, when he descended into the basement mechanical room, he found the source of the malfunction: a corroded coupling on a chlorine tank had fractured, and a yellowish-green cloud was already filling the lower half of the room.

He made it out and called 911, but not before inhaling a significant dose. The next six hours blurred into an ambulance ride, an emergency room, oxygen masks, and a chest that felt as though it had been lined with broken glass. The doctors told him he was fortunate—his exposure was moderate, not severe. No permanent lung damage. He could go home in two days.

But something in Thom's mind had registered differently. He had been in a sealed room with a poison he could not see clearly until it was almost too late. His body had betrayed him by not warning him sooner. The safety protocols everyone relied on—the inspection schedules, the maintenance logs, the assurances from the facility manager that the equipment was "regularly checked"—had all failed. He had come within moments of something far worse.

In the weeks that followed, Thom returned to work, but the world had become a place where invisible threats pooled in corners and seeped under doorways. He began checking the locks on his truck before he drove anywhere. At a client's home, he would test the windows in the basement before descending to the furnace. At night, he would rise from bed three, sometimes four times to verify that the front door was locked, that the garage door was closed, that the basement windows were sealed. His wife, Maria, watched him move through their house like a man searching for something he had already lost.

The tension never left his shoulders. Even when he sat on the couch in the evening, his muscles felt wound tight, as though his body was braced for impact. When Maria suggested they take a weekend trip or sit together on the porch with coffee, Thom would feel a spike of unease. Relaxing meant lowering his guard, and lowering his guard meant something terrible could happen. He had come to believe—despite Maria's gentle reminders, despite his own rational knowledge—that safety was an illusion maintained by people who simply had not yet encountered their moment of exposure.

Being alone made it worse. If he was by himself in a room or a building, the silence seemed to amplify the possibility of danger. He began scheduling his work calls so that he could finish jobs before his colleagues left the office, or he would linger unnecessarily, finding reasons to stay in occupied spaces. When Maria had to travel for her sister's funeral, Thom spent the three nights at his brother's house rather than alone in their home, telling himself it was to help with repairs, but knowing the truth: the thought of being the only person in the house, responsible for detecting any threat, was unbearable.

At fifty-two, Thom had lost the ease that had once defined him. His hands trembled slightly when he held diagnostic equipment. He had turned down the larger jobs that required solo work in unfamiliar buildings. Maria had stopped inviting friends over because Thom's constant vigilance—the checking, the questions about whether the windows were secure, his visible discomfort—made gatherings tense and brief. His supervisor had gently suggested that Thom might benefit from some time off, though the implication was clear: the job was suffering.

It was Maria who finally insisted. She had found him at three in the morning checking the basement windows for the second time that night, his face drawn, his breathing shallow. She said, quietly, that she could not watch him disappear into this fear any longer. Thom had called his doctor the next morning, and now, sitting in the therapist's office, he was trying to articulate something he had never quite named: the certainty that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that his hypervigilance was the only thing standing between his family and catastrophe.
